strengths: Proposes a modular, non-intrusive runtime supervision framework (SupervisorAgent) for multi-agent systems that targets error propagation, inefficient loops, and excessive observations without modifying base agents.
Introduces an LLM-free adaptive filter to trigger supervision only at critical interactions, which helps control the overhead of supervision.

Conducts extensive experiments on the challenging GAIA benchmark plus five additional benchmarks covering math reasoning, code generation, and question answering, and tests multiple foundation models.
Reports substantial token savings (e.g., 29.68% on GAIA with Smolagent) while maintaining competitive average accuracy, and shows reduced token-cost variance.
Includes an ablation study dissecting the contributions of error correction, inefficiency guidance, and observation purification, as well as cross-framework validation on AWorld and OAgents.
The paper is generally clear, with useful figures and a detailed case study illustrating how supervision can improve efficiency and recover from failures.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: runtime supervision, critic/verifier agents, and guard agents are well-known in multi-agent LLM systems; the LLM-free heuristic filter is simple and the overall contribution feels incremental relative to existing supervision and reflection methods.

The paper lacks systematic comparison to existing runtime supervision/reflection approaches (e.g., Reflexion, self-critique, verifier agents) and to efficiency-focused MAS methods such as context compression or agent pruning; AWorld's Guard is compared only in one subset experiment.

Evaluation reporting contains inconsistencies and likely errors: the GAIA split is described as the validation set in Table 1 but as the test set in the appendix; table annotations have incorrect percentages (e.g., pass@2 improvement, Smolagent+SMAS token reduction in Table 4 vs. Table 3); abstract and introduction use different token-reduction numbers (29.45% vs. 29.68%).

No statistical significance tests or confidence intervals are provided for the reported accuracy and token differences, making claims of 'statistically equivalent' success rates and variance reduction insufficiently supported.

The adaptive filter relies on hand-crafted heuristics and thresholds (e.g., 3,000-character length threshold, simple inefficiency detection) whose robustness, false-positive rate, and false-negative rate are not analyzed; generalization to other MAS frameworks may be fragile.

The ablation shows that observation purification drives most token savings but can hurt accuracy on some benchmarks (e.g., DROP, MBPP), while error correction and guidance improve accuracy but not token efficiency; this trade-off is not explored deeply.
Model-agnostic claims are supported only by GAIA experiments with three LLMs; broader validation across benchmarks and models is needed to substantiate generality.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: exact GAIA split, random seeds, implementation of the inefficiency detector, and whether all supervisor token costs are included in reported token counts are unclear.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence, such as 'significant Pareto improvement' despite accuracy drops on some benchmarks and no GAIA pass@1 accuracy gain, and positioning SupervisorAgent as a 'foundational' MAS component is not fully demonstrated.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: token efficiency and robustness in LLM-based multi-agent systems, which is relevant to real-world deployment.
Proposes a modular, non-intrusive runtime supervision framework with an adaptive filter and multiple intervention actions (approve, guidance, correction, verification).
Evaluates on GAIA plus five additional benchmarks and multiple foundation models, reporting some token reductions while mostly maintaining accuracy on the chosen Smolagent baseline.
Includes ablation and cross-framework experiments (AWorld, OAgents), suggesting the approach may be applicable beyond a single MAS architecture.
Provides implementation details and prompts in the appendix, which partially aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: runtime supervisor/critic/guard agents and context-compression methods already exist; AWorld's Guard agent is conceptually similar and the paper does not sufficiently differentiate or benchmark against it.

The main GAIA comparison is not controlled and not competitive: SMAS is applied only to Smolagent, while stronger baselines such as AWorld (60.00% accuracy, 128K tokens) and OAgents (49.09% accuracy, 340K tokens) outperform SMAS (50.91% accuracy, 371K tokens) on full GAIA, undermining the efficiency/robustness claims.

Claims are overstated and numbers are inconsistent: 'statistically equivalent' success rates are reported without significance tests; pass@2/pass@3 improvement percentages appear incorrect (e.g., 58.18 to 58.79 is labeled ↑8.61%); token reduction is 29.45% in the abstract but 29.68% in the intro/conclusion; the appendix says GAIA test set while the main text says validation set.

Ablation and cross-framework evaluations use a small, potentially biased subset (top-10 most token-intensive tasks per GAIA level, ~30 tasks), which likely inflates token savings and limits generality.

No analysis of the adaptive filter: trigger rate, precision/recall, false positives/negatives, or overhead are not reported. It is unclear whether the LLM supervisor's own token cost is fully included in the reported totals.

Missing simple baselines: observation truncation/summarization alone, always-approve, periodic supervision, or existing context-compression methods are not compared. The ablation suggests purification drives most token savings, but a purification-only baseline is not tested.

The robustness/variance claim is weakly supported: only token-cost distributions are shown, with no statistical tests or error analysis. Early truncation could reduce variance at the cost of task success.
Reproducibility is limited: the code link is missing/blank, and there are no seeds, number of runs, detailed cost accounting, or hyperparameter sensitivity analyses.

Formal definitions are superficial and not operationalized; no algorithm pseudocode is provided, and the 'non-intrusive' framing is questionable because the supervisor directly modifies observations and guidance.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: the token inefficiency and brittleness of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS).
Proposes a modular, non-intrusive SupervisorAgent that can be integrated with existing MAS without altering their core architecture.
The LLM-free adaptive filter is a sensible design choice to avoid constant LLM supervision overhead by triggering interventions only at high-risk interaction points.
Experimental coverage is broad: GAIA plus five additional benchmarks, multiple foundation models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-pro, Qwen3), and cross-framework tests on AWorld and OAgents.
Reports substantial token reductions (e.g., 29.68% on GAIA with Smolagent, 23.74% on HumanEval) and reduced token-cost variance, which is valuable for practical deployment.
Includes ablation studies and a case study, and provides prompts/implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: runtime supervision, guard agents, self-reflection, and process verification for MAS are already studied; the core idea of an LLM supervisor that corrects/guides/purifies observations is incremental.

No direct comparison against existing efficiency-oriented MAS methods such as AgentDropout, SafeSieve, or context-compression baselines, despite these being discussed in related work. The main efficiency comparison is only against the base Smolagent system.

Accuracy claims are stronger than the evidence: the abstract/intro claim "without compromising success rate," but GAIA Level 2 accuracy drops (53.49→51.16 at pass@1; 59.30→56.98 at pass@2), and DROP/MBPP also show accuracy drops in Table 2.

Token accounting is unclear: it is not specified whether the reported token consumption includes the SupervisorAgent's own LLM calls, verification sub-agent calls, and prompt overhead. Without this breakdown, the net efficiency gain is not fully established.

The ablation study is conducted only on a small, non-representative subset (top-10 most token-intensive tasks per level), and the full-GAIA results do not mirror the subset accuracy gains. The ablation table is also confusing and partially contradicts the textual interpretation.
Cross-framework experiments are limited to the same small subset, and some reported relative gains contain typos (e.g., 40.00→46.67 is labeled as ↑0.67% in Table 4).
The adaptive filter relies on simple heuristic thresholds (e.g., 3,000 characters, loop detection) with no sensitivity analysis or learning; it may be brittle across domains and datasets.

Evaluation protocol has inconsistencies: the main text says GAIA validation set, while the appendix says test set with 164 tasks; pass@k protocol and token measurement are not fully specified; no statistical significance tests are reported.
The paper acknowledges that aggressive observation purification can harm performance due to "noise-as-signal" but offers no principled solution beyond tuning.
Reproducibility is incomplete: the code link is missing/truncated in the provided manuscript, and key hyperparameters/implementation details are only partially specified.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: improving efficiency and robustness of LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) without altering base agent architectures.

Proposes a modular runtime supervision framework (SupervisorAgent) with an adaptive filter and a multi-level action space, covering error correction, inefficiency guidance, and observation purification.

Conducts extensive experiments on GAIA and five additional benchmarks (math reasoning, code generation, QA), across multiple foundation models, and includes cross-framework integration, ablations, overhead analysis, and failure mode analysis.
Reports substantial token savings on GAIA (29.68% at pass@1) while maintaining average success, and some accuracy gains on hard subsets (e.g., GAIA top-token-intensive tasks).
Provides detailed implementation descriptions, hyperparameters, prompts, and case studies, which aid reproducibility in principle.
Transparently discusses limitations, failure modes, and trade-offs, which is a positive scientific practice.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: runtime supervision/critic/guard agents already exist in the literature (e.g., AWorld Guard), and the proposed adaptive filter relies on simple heuristics (step interval, loop detection, length threshold) rather than a novel learning or algorithmic contribution.

The individual intervention strategies (error correction, guidance, observation purification) are intuitive and not fundamentally new; the main contribution is an engineering combination with empirical validation.

Evaluation inconsistencies: the appendix states they use the GAIA test set (164 tasks), but Table 1 refers to the GAIA validation set; since GAIA test answers are private, this raises serious reproducibility and validity concerns. The code URL is also missing.

The main claim of 'without compromising success rate' is not fully supported: on GAIA Level 2 at pass@1 and pass@2, accuracy drops (53.49→51.16 and 59.30→56.98), and the overall average is maintained only due to Level 3 gains that may be noise given small task counts per level.
No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed variance are reported; many accuracy changes on additional benchmarks are within noise (e.g., MBPP -1.25, DROP -1.28).
Cross-framework evaluation on AWorld and OAgents is only on a small subset (top-10 most token-intensive tasks per GAIA level), not the full benchmark, so generality claims are weakly supported.

Missing simple baselines: no comparison to naive context truncation/summarization or standard self-correction/reflection methods, making it difficult to isolate the benefit of the proposed selective supervision.

The method is not competitive with state-of-the-art efficient MAS: AWorld achieves 60.00 average accuracy with 128K tokens on GAIA, far better than Smolagent+SMAS (50.91, 371K); the paper does not integrate SMAS into AWorld on full GAIA.
The adaptive filter triggers supervision at fixed step intervals regardless of actual inefficiency, potentially adding overhead; no ablation isolates this trigger's effect.
The 'memory-augmented' context window is essentially inclusion of the global trace, not a true memory module, so the terminology overclaims the mechanism.

Supervisor overhead averages 15.45% of total tokens, and latency increases by 37.27% (about 1.5 minutes per task), which may be significant for real-time MAS; the time-cost trade-off is not deeply analyzed.
Reproducibility is limited by the missing code link, inconsistent dataset naming, lack of seeds/temperature details, and per-benchmark hyperparameter tuning that may not generalize.
The title 'Stop Wasting Your Tokens' overstates the impact given modest savings on several benchmarks (e.g., 5.60% on DROP, 6.62% on MBPP) and the existence of more token-efficient systems.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: efficiency and robustness of LLM-based multi-agent systems.
Proposes a modular runtime supervision framework that can be integrated without altering the base agent architecture.
Provides a clear formalism for Supervised Multi-Agent Systems and a well-defined action space for interventions.
Conducts experiments across six benchmarks and multiple foundation models, reporting token savings and accuracy.
Includes ablation studies, overhead analysis, and a discussion of failure modes.
The LLM-free adaptive filter is a practical idea to reduce the cost of continuous supervision.
Reports substantial token reductions (e.g., 29.68% average on GAIA) and reduced token variance, showing potential for cost savings.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: runtime supervision, critic, and guard agents already exist (e.g., AWorld Guard); the paper does not sufficiently differentiate its contribution or compare against other proactive self-critique/reflection methods.

Evaluation has serious inconsistencies: GAIA is described as both a validation set and a test set; accuracy changes are mislabeled (e.g., 58.79 vs. 58.18 called an 8.61% improvement); 'without compromising success rate' is contradicted by the L2 pass@1 drop (53.49 to 51.16) and accuracy drops on MBPP and DROP.

Lack of statistical significance testing: claims of 'statistically equivalent' success rates and 'variance reduction' are unsupported. Robustness is defined as token consumption variance, not task success robustness.

The adaptive filter's hyperparameters are manually tuned per benchmark (Table 5), undermining claims of adaptivity and generalizability. There is no ablation comparing the filter to always/never supervising, and sensitivity analysis covers only one threshold.

Net overhead accounting is unclear: Table 6 reports both 'Supervised MAS' and 'Supervised MAS (NET)' without clear definitions, and the reported overhead percentage (15.45%) is inconsistent with the implied difference.

Reproducibility issues: the code URL is missing ('available at .'), random seeds and number of runs are not reported, token counting is unspecified, and hyperparameters are tuned on benchmark subsets.
The pass@k metric for GAIA is non-standard and not clearly defined (multiple runs? top-k?); baselines are only evaluated at pass@1, making comparisons unfair.
Cross-framework adaptation to AWorld uses a different MCP-based mechanism with mandatory invocation, so it is not a clean test of the same SupervisorAgent.
Failure mode analysis is anecdotal and lacks quantitative evaluation.
Clarity and writing issues: numerous typos, inconsistent numbers across tables and text, and dense presentation that obscures key details.
Limited comparison to strong efficiency baselines: methods such as self-refine, Reflexion, context compression, and AgentDropout are not compared.
Latency overhead is significant (37.27% increase) and not fully analyzed; the trade-off may be unacceptable for real-time or latency-sensitive applications.
Potential ethical/safety implications of a supervisor modifying observations and guiding agents are not discussed, including the risk of the supervisor introducing new errors.

strengths: Introduces a practical runtime supervision framework for MAS that is modular and non-intrusive, targeting error propagation, inefficient loops, and excessive observations.
Demonstrates substantial token savings on GAIA and five additional benchmarks, with ablations isolating the contributions of correction, guidance, and purification.
Evaluates across multiple foundation models (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5-pro, Qwen3) and MAS frameworks, showing broad applicability.
Provides detailed implementation, prompts, hyperparameters, and overhead/latency analyses, supporting reproducibility.
Addresses a timely problem (efficiency and robustness of multi-agent LLM systems) with clear practical relevance.
weaknesses: The GAIA evaluation split is inconsistent: main text says validation set, while Appendix A.2.1 says test set (164 tasks); this must be clarified as it affects validity/reproducibility.

The main efficiency gains likely stem from observation purification/compression, but the paper does not compare against direct context-compression/summarization baselines, making it unclear whether the full supervision framework is necessary.
The 'adaptive' filter relies on manually tuned heuristics and per-benchmark thresholds, and the sensitivity analysis is limited, so adaptivity/generalizability claims are not fully supported.
Claims of 'without compromising success rate' are overstated: accuracy drops on GAIA Level 2 for pass@1/2/3, and F1 drops on DROP and MBPP; no statistical significance tests are reported.

The cross-framework evaluation uses a small token-intensive subset and contains apparent reporting errors (e.g., accuracy improvement shown as ↑0.67% when 40.00→46.67 is +6.67%), weakening those conclusions.
Latency overhead is substantial (avg. +37.27%, up to +49.59% on Level 1), which may limit real-time applicability despite token savings.
The core idea of a supervisor/guard agent is related to existing work (e.g., AWorld Guard); the novelty is incremental without deeper theoretical or algorithmic innovation.
The reproducibility statement omits the actual code URL, and some implementation choices (e.g., hard two-guidance limit) may affect reported robustness.
